title: ASIC halts two private credit funds over PDS, Bathla disclosure concerns
full_text:
The corporate regulator has halted the sales of two funds by Angas Securities over concerns on the product disclosure statements not adequately disclosing the firm's financial position and one fund's exposure to the Bathla Group.
The interim stop orders prevent Angas Securities from offering, issuing, selling, or transferring interests in the Angas Prime Income Fund and the Angas Direct Mortgage Fund.
ASIC is concerned investors in both funds may not have been adequately informed about the financial position of the firm and the risks arising from that position. It is also concerned about disclosures of Angas Prime Income Fund relating to its exposure to the collapsed Bathla Group.
"Our message to private credit fund managers is crystal clear," ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said.
"Investors need clear and timely information about the risks they are taking on, particularly when circumstances change and private credit loans run into difficulty.
"The collapse of the Bathla Group has highlighted the risks that can emerge in private credit when this message is ignored. The Bathla collapse drives home the importance of strong governance, appropriate valuations and clear disclosure to private credit investors."
ASIC has been coming down heavy on the private credit sector, recently hitting funds by Murdoch Clarke Mortgage Management and Fidante Partners with stop orders over lack of proper disclosures.
Late September, Constant said the regulator was "beyond warnings" and pushed private credit players to assess themselves against its 10 best practice principles.
She urged the sector to uplift standards, noting participants should prepare for enforcement action if they fail to do so.
ASIC said it will consider whether final stop orders should be made after giving Angas Securities an opportunity to be heard.
In August, property developer Bathla Group went into voluntary administration, raising fears that investors will pull back from private credit funds exposed to the sector.
"ASIC is engaging closely with voluntary administrators to trace the $3.2 billion in funds loaned to Bathla and making a range of inquiries focused on taking further action as appropriate. One of our main concerns is to understand the extent to which there are retail investors affected," Constant said.
"ASIC will continue its broader scrutiny of private credit and will continue to step up our actions. We will act swiftly where we are concerned investors are not being given the full picture about the risks they face."
